sec.h: WOUND HEALING (asked repeatedly in multiple forms — master fully)
b: Sequence of cutaneous wound healing:
Haemostasis — blood clot formation (first event)
Inflammation — neutrophils then macrophages clear debris
Proliferation — granulation tissue forms (fibroblasts + macrophages + new capillaries/angiogenesis), re-epithelialisation occurs
Remodelling — collagen type III replaced by stronger type I, scar matures, wound contracts

o: Development of an ulcer at the site
qs.e: Wound dehiscence is a recognized complication of cutaneous wound healing.

qs.q: A patient presents with bleeding gums, impaired wound healing, and petechiae. These symptoms are most consistent with a deficiency in which vitamin?
qs.e: These symptoms are classic signs of scurvy, caused by a deficiency of Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid). Vitamin C is crucial for collagen synthesis, acting as a cofactor for hydroxylase enzymes involved in forming stable collagen helices.

qs.q: Which trace mineral functions as a cofactor for numerous enzymes, supports immune function, and is involved in wound healing?
qs.e: Zinc is an essential trace mineral that acts as a cofactor for over 300 enzymes involved in diverse metabolic processes. It plays crucial roles in immune function, wound healing, DNA synthesis, and cell division.

qs.q: Wound healing is affected by all of the following EXCEPT:
qs.e: Vitamin C deficiency (nutrition), infection, and steroids (glucocorticoids) significantly impair healing. Blood group (A, B, O) has no impact on the healing process.

qs.q: Wound healing involves all the processes outlined below EXCEPT:

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Wound healing is a dynamic, staged process that restores skin integrity after injury. It requires coordinated cellular, molecular, and systemic factors, and failure at any stage can lead to chronic wounds or excessive scarring.

sections.p: Wound healing describes the orderly progression from haemostasis to remodeling that restores the skin barrier after trauma.
b: Diagnosed clinically by observing the wound edge, granulation tissue, and scar formation over time.

sections.p: Stages are haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling; severity is graded by depth (superficial, partial‑thickness, full‑thickness) and by presence of infection or ischemia.
b: Full‑thickness wounds need more aggressive care and may need grafting.

sections.p: Wounds arise from trauma, surgery, pressure, or disease. In low‑resource settings, added causes include chronic infections (TB, leprosy), vascular disease (sickle cell, peripheral arterial disease), and traditional remedies that impair healing.
b: Mechanical trauma (lacerations, abrasions)
Surgical incisions
Pressure ulcers
Infection (bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal)
Vascular insufficiency (diabetes, sickle cell)
Nutritional deficiency (protein, zinc, vitamin C)
Medications that impair collagen (steroids, chemotherapy)

sections.p: Acute wounds show a predictable colour change: red, moist granulation then pink epithelialization. Chronic wounds stay inflamed, have foul odor, and may show necrotic tissue.
b: Pain and erythema early (inflammation)
Yellow‑white granulation tissue in proliferation
Hard, pale scar in remodeling

sections.p: Tests identify infection, perfusion, and systemic factors that hinder repair.

t.b: Is there pathogenic bacteria? Guides antibiotic choice; if unavailable, treat empirically based on local flora.
Is arterial perfusion adequate? Low ABI (<0.9) suggests ischemia needing revascularization.
Is nutritional status sufficient? Low values predict delayed healing; start supplementation.
Is glycemic control poor? >7% indicates need for tighter control to improve healing.

sections.p: Complications arise when any stage is disrupted, leading to infection, necrosis, or hypertrophic scarring.
b: Rapid expansion of erythema or pain → cellulitis or necrotizing fasciitis
Foul odor, purulent discharge → deep infection
Wound edge necrosis → tissue loss
Excessive granulation (proud flesh) → may need debridement

sections.p: Treat underlying cause, optimise systemic factors, and provide local wound care.
b: Debridement of necrotic tissue (surgical, enzymatic, autolytic)
Moist dressings (hydrocolloid, alginate) to promote granulation
Topical antimicrobials (silver sulfadiazine, honey) for contaminated wounds
Systemic antibiotics for proven infection; choose agents covering Staph aureus and Gram‑negatives, avoid prolonged use to prevent resistance
Nutritional support: protein 1.2‑1.5 g/kg, zinc 15‑30 mg/day, vitamin C 500 mg/day
Control diabetes, improve perfusion (revascularization, compression for venous ulcers)
Consider negative‑pressure wound therapy for large, complex wounds

sections.p: Regular reassessment ensures progression through stages and early detection of complications.
b: Inspect wounds every 2‑3 days; document size, depth, exudate
Educate patients on off‑loading, hygiene, and nutrition
Vaccinate against tetanus; screen for HIV/TB in high‑risk areas

sections.p: Conditions that mimic poor healing can mislead clinicians.
b: Chronic dermatitis (inflammation without true tissue loss)
Vasculitic ulcers (immune‑mediated, not purely mechanical)
Neoplastic ulceration (cancer invasion)

sections.p: Laboratory or clinical signs may appear normal despite ongoing pathology.
b: Normal white count in early infection of immunocompromised patients
Normal ABI in calcified vessels (false‑negative); use toe‑brachial index
Serum zinc may be normal despite functional deficiency; assess clinical signs

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid spreading redness or pain beyond wound margins
Signs of systemic toxicity (tachycardia, hypotension, altered mental status)

faq.q: Why is a moist environment better for wound healing?
faq.a: Moisture prevents desiccation, supports cell migration, and promotes angiogenesis, leading to faster epithelialization.

faq.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary intention healing?
faq.a: Primary intention closes a clean wound with sutures, resulting in minimal scar; secondary intention leaves the wound open to granulate, producing more scar.

faq.q: How does diabetes impair wound healing?
faq.a: Hyperglycemia reduces neutrophil function, impairs collagen synthesis, and causes microvascular disease, all slowing the repair process.
